title: Lifting Multiplicity in Randomized Benchmarking
abstract: Randomized benchmarking comprises a suite of standard techniques for assessing the operational fidelity of quantum processors. These techniques can be reliably applied to groups with process matrix representations that are free of multiplicity. However, many groups that are naturally formed from native gates do have multiplicity, and it is difficult to draw robust conclusions from the resulting data. In this work, we present a new and intrinsic solution to the problem of multiplicity that completely eliminates the need to fit multi-exponential decays while still remaining robust to errors in state preparation and measurement. Our procedure, which we call lifted randomized benchmarking, generalizes key elements of both character and synthetic randomized benchmarking to benchmark a target group of quantum gates with respect to an enlarged group. We illustrate in numerical examples that our method can efficiently and reliably estimate the fidelity of two-qubit gates relevant to experimental trapped-ion systems. These techniques may find applications beyond randomized benchmarking to quantum tomography and learning, as well as the characterization of error-correcting codes.
summary: This paper introduces Lifted Randomized Benchmarking, a theoretical advancement for assessing quantum gate fidelity. It solves the problem where native gate groups have multiplicity, which complicates data analysis by requiring multi-exponential fits. By enlarging the benchmarking group to a multiplicity-free structure, the method allows for robust fidelity estimation using only single exponential fits.
main_problem: Standard Randomized Benchmarking fails when the group of native quantum gates has multiplicity, leading to complex data requiring multi-exponential fits.
main_result: The authors introduce 'Lifted Randomized Benchmarking,' a method that estimates gate fidelity by fitting only single exponential decays, thereby bypassing the need to handle multiplicity.
method: The technique generalizes character and synthetic RB by enlarging the benchmarking group to a larger, multiplicity-free group, allowing the estimation of decay rates via single exponential fits.
model_or_system: The theory applies to assessing the operational fidelity of quantum processors, specifically illustrated using two-qubit gates relevant to trapped-ion systems.
key_observables: Average weighted survival probabilities (e.g., p_Lambda^m) and the eigenvalues of the noise-related matrix M_lambda(E).
important_parameters: The choice of the auxiliary lifting group F, which must contain the isotypic component of the target representation.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a suitable lifting group F and is robust to errors in state preparation and measurement (SPAM).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first identifying the failure mode (multiplicity in RB), then proposing the lifting procedure by enlarging the group, and finally demonstrating its application to estimate fidelity for specific physical gate sets.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, general theoretical tool for characterizing quantum hardware performance that circumvents known mathematical bottlenecks (multiplicity) in standard benchmarking protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Performance of lifted randomized benchmarking with gate-independent noise over varying noise channel infidelities, circuits per depth, and shots per circuit. These fits were constructed over the geometric interval 2k with maximum depth 64, N circuits per depth, and S shots per circuit. Each point represents the median of 20 trials of the lifting benchmarking protocol for a given noise channel, and the error bars represent the central 68% intervals. Each element of the lifting group and benchmarking group has the same noise channel. We find that for N = 1000, some of the fits fail and produce estimates with infidelity less than 0, and for the others with greater circuits per depth,...

Figure 2: Estimated fidelity with noisy lifting vs. perfect lifting. We apply our procedure for the ZZ gate with 10,000 circuits per depth and 100 shots per circuit. Each point represents the median of 20 trials of the lifting benchmarking protocol for a given noise channel, and the error bars represent the central 68% intervals. In the case of perfect lifting, perfect lifting operators are applied (which means that only the last lifting operator that was not compiled into the benchmarking sequence is perfect). Figure 3: Estimated poles of the ZZ gate error channel in the complex plane. A single noise channel was fixed at the beginning of the experiment, and each point represents an experimental implementation with that fixed noise channel. The ZZ gate benchmarking group projects a general CPTP noise process onto the irrep decomposition, and our procedure robustly measures the eigenvalues of the isotypic components. These fits were constructed over the geometric interval 2k with maximum depth 64, N circuits per depth, and 1000 shots per circuit.

Figure 4: MS gate benchmarking results for gate-independent noise. Each point represents the median of 20 trials of the lifting benchmarking protocol over a given noise channel, and the error bars represent the central 68% intervals. The error channels consist of equal parts Pauli stochastic and coherent noise.

Figure 5: Estimated poles of the MS gate error channel in the complex plane. A single noise channel was fixed at the beginning of the experiment, and each point represents an experimental implementation with that fixed noise channel. The MS gate benchmarking group projects a general CPTP noise process onto the irrep decomposition, and our procedure robustly measures the eigenvalues of the isotypic components. These fits were constructed over the geometric interval 2k with maximum depth 64, N circuits per depth, and 1000 shots per circuit.
